items.prompt: Which of these is formal seniority?
choices: A title and a place on the org chart
Knowing a tool better than others
Being the best presenter on the team
Being liked by most colleagues
items.explanation: Formal seniority is what shows up on paper: title, tenure, pay band, org-chart position.

items.prompt: Renee built the postmortem practice. What kind of seniority does that give her?
choices: Formal seniority over Jordan's whole role
Authority over Jordan's calibration input
A higher title than the one Jordan holds
Domain seniority on that one practice
items.explanation: Building the practice makes her the person who knows it best, which is domain seniority and nothing more.

items.prompt: Who writes Renee's calibration input this cycle?
choices: Renee herself, as the practice's author
Her skip-level manager, alone
Jordan, who joined three weeks ago
The whole team, by an open vote
items.explanation: Jordan's role in her review is part of why the gap feels risky.

items.prompt: Jordan has ten years of experience. What does that tell you about postmortems here?
choices: That he is already an expert at this exact format here
Nothing certain; experience is not this practice
That Renee's method is flawed or out of date
That he will learn the format far more quickly than anyone
items.explanation: Tenure is formal seniority. It says little about a practice he has never run in this team.

items.prompt: Which statement about the two kinds of seniority is true?
choices: They can point in opposite directions for the same pair
They always match in a healthy team
Domain seniority is just a politer title
Formal seniority always implies deeper skill
items.explanation: Renee and Jordan are the unit's example of the two diverging.

items.prompt: What does domain seniority cover?
choices: Every task a person might ever do at work
The person's pay band and formal level
Whom the person reports to in the company
One specific skill, not everything
items.explanation: Domain seniority is narrow: Renee's edge covers postmortems only.

items.prompt: Which sentence names a domain-seniority fact?
choices: Jordan sits two levels above Renee on the chart
Jordan's years in the industry
Renee knows how to run a blameless postmortem here
Jordan will write Renee's review input this cycle, as it stands now
items.explanation: Only the first is about who knows the skill; the rest are formal facts.

items.prompt: Peer mentoring is mostly about what?
choices: Teaching only the people who report directly to you
Teaching someone ahead of you on paper
Teaching only colleagues who hold exactly your title
Helping a manager assess your team's performance
items.explanation: It covers equals and formal superiors, where the org chart gives you no teaching role.

items.prompt: Renee says 'I know this practice better, so I'm more senior than Jordan here.' What is wrong with that statement?
choices: It is accurate, because knowledge outranks title in any team where skills are visible
It stretches a narrow skill edge into overall standing
It confuses tenure with calibration input, which Renee has no part in at all
It would only be wrong if Jordan had already run a postmortem here before today
items.explanation: Her edge is real but narrow. Turning it into overall seniority is the overreach that makes corrections feel like challenges.
items.reference:
Two gradients, one pair of people
📋 Formal: title, tenure, calibration input (Jordan ahead)
🛠️ Domain: running this postmortem practice (Renee ahead)
↔️ They point in opposite directions
Why: one seniority number cannot describe two people who each lead on a different dimension.
items.learnMore:
Formal versus domain seniority

Formal seniority is what shows on paper: title, tenure, pay band, org-chart position. Domain seniority is who actually knows a specific skill better. Mentoring models often assume the two coincide; peer mentoring exists for the cases where they do not.

Common mistake

Treating the more senior title as the person who knows more about everything.
items.reflection: Think of a colleague who outranked you but knew less about one thing you knew well. What did that gap look like day to day?

items.prompt: Jordan has a higher title, more years and writes Renee's input. Which conclusion does that support?
choices: He must also be ahead of her on running this exact postmortem format here
He should defer to her on everything involving incidents, given her record
His calibration input should be set aside on incident topics
He is ahead of her on formal dimensions only
items.explanation: All three listed facts are formal. None of them says anything about knowing this particular practice.

Her expertise goes unused
Jordan stops writing her review input

He will always thank her for the clarity
The postmortem will run itself better
Her tenure will count for more

choices: A person's exact salary band this year
The number of meetings they attend each week
How others see and respect a person

items.prompt: Which is a silence failure?
choices: Renee offers a walkthrough and Jordan declines
Renee sees the gap and says nothing
Renee names one practice and leaves the choice open to him
Renee credits Jordan's incident experience

items.prompt: Which is a clumsy-correction failure?

Renee asks first and scopes the offer
Renee lets Jordan decide how to use it, after she explains
Renee waits until Jordan asks for help
items.explanation: The tone and audience turn information into a challenge.

items.prompt: Does a correct correction always land well?
choices: Yes; being right is all that matters
Yes, as long as it is said loudly
No, but only when the facts are wrong
No; accuracy does not guarantee it is heard as help
items.explanation: The unit's point is that a true correction can still be heard as a challenge.

items.prompt: What is the way out of the two failure modes?
choices: Always staying silent in the future
Always correcting as soon as you notice any gap
A scoped offer where the other person decides
Waiting until your own title catches up
items.explanation: Framing, not courage, is what separates help from a challenge.

items.prompt: Renee stays quiet and Jordan runs a weak postmortem. Who bears the first cost?
choices: Only Renee, through a lower calibration score
Only Jordan, through a lost title
The team, which misses what Renee already knows
Nobody, since a weak postmortem has no cost
items.explanation: Silence feels safe for the quiet person, but the lost knowledge lands on the team.
items.reference:
Two ways to lose
🤐 Silence: expertise unused, team learns less
📣 Clumsy correction: reads as disrespect for the org chart
✅ Scoped offer: names one practice, leaves the decision
Why: both failures are avoidable, and the way out is framing, not courage.
items.learnMore:
The cost of correcting upward

A correction from someone ahead of you carries little social risk. From someone behind you on paper, it can sound like a challenge to standing, even when accurate. That asymmetry is what makes staying silent tempting.

Common mistake

Believing the only choices are staying quiet or saying it bluntly.
items.reflection: When did you last stay quiet about something you knew, or say it too bluntly? Which cost showed up first?

None, because accuracy alone settles how it is received
The correction will turn out to be wrong for some other reason
Jordan will lose tenure on the org chart
items.explanation: Right content in a public, unscoped delivery can still be read as disrespect.

Renee's direct manager at her company
Jordan's predecessor on the team

items.prompt: Renee tells Jordan, 'I've noticed you're still getting used to how things work here, so let me show you the ropes.' Which move does that break?

items.explanation: 'How things work here' reaches well beyond her one practice, however warm the tone.
items.reference:
The four moves
1️⃣ Ask, don't announce
2️⃣ Scope it narrowly
3️⃣ Credit what they bring
4️⃣ Let them keep the decision
Why: each move limits what Renee claims, so the help does not read as a bid for standing.
items.learnMore:
Scope is the real lever

An unscoped correction claims authority over how someone works. A scoped one claims authority over a single practice you actually know. The four moves keep the claim exactly as large as the knowledge behind it.

Common mistake

Treating the problem as tone only and trusting a softer voice to fix an overbroad claim.
